cards.explanation: The chief priests, scribes and elders want to know by what authority Jesus does these things. They ask Him, “By what authority are You doing these things?” and then add, “And who gave You the authority to do them?” (Mark 11:28). That's two questions stacked in one breath. Hold onto your apron, friends, because Jesus is about to turn the conversation around.

Jesus says He'll tell them by what authority He acts. He says, “and if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” (Mark 11:29). So He sets up a trade: their answer first, His answer after. Notice He doesn't dodge them. He just picks the order.

The two choices are from heaven or from men. Jesus asks about John, the one who baptized people, and puts it this way: “…was it from heaven or from men?” (Mark 11:30). Two choices, no third door. I think that's why this question feels like a tight squeeze.

They think Jesus will ask why they didn't believe John. They say it themselves: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’” (Mark 11:31). They can see the trap closing before they step in it. I do that with a text I'm about to send: type it, read it back, and see the reply coming before I ever hit send.

The answer is False. There are no soldiers in this part of the story. The text says, “they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John truly was a prophet.” (Mark 11:32). The crowd's opinion of John is what boxes the leaders in.

The leaders answer, “We do not know.” (Mark 11:33). They had two doors and chose to say neither. Honestly, friends, I've given that shrug in a staff meeting when both answers got me in trouble, and it never helped me either.

The answer is True. Jesus holds to the deal He made. He replies, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” (Mark 11:33). No answer from the leaders, no answer from Him. It's a fair trade, and they're the ones who left it empty.

The owner rents the vineyard to tenants and goes on a journey. Jesus says the man “…rented it out to some tenants and went away on a journey.” (Mark 12:1). So the owner rents the vineyard out and travels away. Remember who's in that vineyard, friends, because it matters soon.

The tenants beat the servant and send him away empty-handed. Jesus says, “But they seized the servant, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.” (Mark 12:3). The servant came for the owner's share and left with nothing. That's a hard turn in the story.

The answer is False. The owner doesn't stop sending people. Jesus says, “He sent still another, and this one they killed. He sent many others; some they beat and others they killed.” (Mark 12:5). It's a heavy part of the story.

The one the owner sends is his beloved son. Jesus says, “Finally, having one beloved son, he sent him to them.” (Mark 12:6). The word “one” stands out to me. After all those servants, this is the last one the owner sends in the story.

The owner expects the tenants to respect his son. He says, “They will respect my son…” (Mark 12:6). He sends his son expecting a better welcome than the servants got. I think that hope is what makes the next verse hit so hard.

The tenants think they'll get the inheritance. They say, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” (Mark 12:7). They know exactly who he is. I think that's a dark plan.

The word that fills the blank is vineyard. Jesus says, “So they seized the son, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.” (Mark 12:8). The vineyard is the same place the owner planted and walled in at the start. It's a heavy moment in the parable.

The owner will kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others. Jesus answers His own question: “He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” (Mark 12:9). It's a hard line, and the passage doesn't soften it. The vineyard goes to others.

The rejected stone becomes the cornerstone. Jesus quotes, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” (Mark 12:10). The builders tossed it aside, and it became the most important stone. I've been set aside in a drawer myself, friends, so I like this verse more than most.

The answer is True. The Scripture says, “This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes…” (Mark 12:11). So the stone's new place is from the Lord. The Scripture also calls it marvelous. That's the end of what Jesus quotes.

Jesus spoke the parable against the leaders themselves. The text says, “…they knew that He had spoken this parable against them.” (Mark 12:12). They don't need a map to see where it points. Some stories land so close to home you could mail them there.

What holds the leaders back is fear of the crowd. The text says, “But fearing the crowd, they left Him and went away.” (Mark 12:12). Back in their huddle about John, they were “…afraid of the people…” (Mark 11:32). Fear of the crowd is what holds them back here.
